content: On February 1, 2016, the World Health Organization (WHO) declared a Public Health Emergency of International Concern following reports of clusters of microcephaly, Guillain-Barré syndrome, and other neurological conditions in areas affected by Zika virus transmission. Since late 2015, northeastern Brazil has reported up to a 20-fold increase in congenital microcephaly cases. By August 18, 2016, 17 countries or territories had reported cases of microcephaly and/or central nervous system malformations potentially linked to Zika virus infection. Notably, three countries reported microcephaly in neonates born to mothers who had traveled to Zika-affected regions but resided in areas without endemic Zika transmission. The purpose of this document is to provide updated guidance on the screening, clinical assessment, neuroimaging, and laboratory investigations for neonates and infants born to women in areas of Zika virus transmission. This guidance builds upon WHO’s interim recommendations from March 4, 2016, and includes recent evidence, operational considerations, and recommendations to inform national and local clinical protocols and health policies. It is not intended as a comprehensive guide for managing Zika virus infections or neonatal neurological conditions, including microcephaly. Microcephaly is defined as a condition where a baby’s head circumference is smaller than expected for their age and sex, reflecting reduced intracranial volume and brain growth. Microcephaly present at birth often indicates underlying brain pathology and is associated with developmental delays, intellectual impairment, hearing and vision loss, and epilepsy. However, reliable data on the prevalence of congenital microcephaly remain limited. In the context of Zika virus transmission, congenital Zika virus syndrome encompasses a range of manifestations, including craniofacial disproportion, spasticity, seizures, irritability, brainstem dysfunction, limb contractures, hearing and ocular abnormalities, and brain anomalies detected via neuroimaging. Neuroimaging findings commonly include cortical or subcortical calcifications, cortical malformations, simplified gyral patterns, brainstem or cerebellar hypoplasia, and ventriculomegaly. These abnormalities suggest that Zika virus directly interferes with fetal brain development, either by infecting the brain or the placenta. Emerging evidence strongly supports Zika virus as a cause of microcephaly and other neurological complications, collectively termed congenital Zika virus syndrome. Neonates should also be evaluated for craniofacial disproportion and other signs of congenital Zika virus syndrome. Mothers should be asked about symptoms or laboratory confirmation of Zika virus infection during pregnancy, including the timing of infection. Neuroimaging is recommended for neonates with head circumferences below -2 standard deviations (SD) or with disproportionately small heads relative to the face, particularly if Zika virus infection is suspected during pregnancy or if neurological signs are present. Computed tomography (CT) or magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can identify typical radiological features of congenital Zika virus syndrome, with MRI offering higher resolution for cortical and posterior fossa abnormalities. Cranial ultrasound may be used if CT or MRI is unavailable, but its utility may be limited by the size of the anterior fontanelle. Congenital Zika virus syndrome may also involve sensorineural hearing loss and vision abnormalities. Early hearing screening, preferably before hospital discharge, is essential and should follow WHO guidelines. Vision assessment may require ophthalmological examination, as clinical evaluation during the newborn period can be challenging. Identifying the underlying cause of microcephaly is critical for prognosis, management, and counseling for future pregnancies. A thorough clinical history, physical examination, and laboratory testing can help differentiate congenital infections, such as cytomegalovirus (CMV), from genetic or environmental causes. However, there is currently no validated laboratory test to confirm congenital Zika virus infection in neonates. Zika virus RNA has been detected in neonates with perinatal transmission using reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR), but further diagnostic advancements are needed. In summary, comprehensive evaluation and follow-up of neonates born to mothers with suspected or confirmed Zika virus infection during pregnancy are essential to detect and manage complications associated with congenital Zika virus syndrome.
